title: How do you iterate over AWS resources (e.g. EC2 instances) with Boto3 — the `describe_instances()` → `Reservations` → `Instances` structure — and what must a PRODUCTION script add beyond the happy path (pagination, error handling, filtering, logging, and credentials via the IAM role / credential-provider chain rather than hardcoded keys)?
shortTitle: Iterating over AWS resources with Boto3 and what a production script must add beyond the happy path

s1_definition.profdef: With Boto3 you list EC2 instances by calling `ec2_client.describe_instances()`, which returns a nested structure where the top-level `Reservations` list contains `Instances` lists, so you iterate reservations and then instances within each. A toy script stops there, but a production script must additionally handle pagination so it never silently drops results, catch and classify errors so transient failures are retried and permission failures are surfaced, filter server-side so it transfers only what it needs, log structured progress for audit, and obtain credentials through the default credential-provider chain (an IAM role) rather than hardcoding access keys.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India asks for a list of all its cars (EC2 instances). The simple clerk calls the garage once and reads the first page of the list — but the garage only hands over one page at a time and says "there are more" (pagination), and the simple clerk misses them. A professional clerk keeps asking until there are no more pages, writes down what went wrong if the phone drops (error handling and retries), asks the garage to pre-filter to only the production cars instead of hauling the whole list home (server-side filtering), keeps a logbook of everything done (logging), and uses the bank's official ID badge rather than a photocopied key taped to the wall (IAM role instead of hardcoded keys).
s1_definition.oneliner: Iterate `Reservations` then `Instances`, but in production add paginators, error handling with retries, server-side filters, structured logging, and credentials from the IAM role chain — never hardcoded keys.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** With Boto3 you list EC2 instances by calling `ec2_client.describe_instances()`, which returns a nested structure where the top-level `Reservations` list contains `Instances` lists, so you iterate reservations and then instances within each. A toy script stops there, but a production script must additionally handle pagination so it never silently drops results, catch and classify errors so transient failures are retried and permission failures are surfaced, filter server-side so it transfers only what it needs, log structured progress for audit, and obtain credentials through the default credential-provider chain (an IAM role) rather than hardcoding access keys.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India asks for a list of all its cars (EC2 instances). The simple clerk calls the garage once and reads the first page of the list — but the garage only hands over one page at a time and says "there are more" (pagination), and the simple clerk misses them. A professional clerk keeps asking until there are no more pages, writes down what went wrong if the phone drops (error handling and retries), asks the garage to pre-filter to only the production cars instead of hauling the whole list home (server-side filtering), keeps a logbook of everything done (logging), and uses the bank's official ID badge rather than a photocopied key taped to the wall (IAM role instead of hardcoded keys).

**One line to remember:** Iterate `Reservations` then `Instances`, but in production add paginators, error handling with retries, server-side filters, structured logging, and credentials from the IAM role chain — never hardcoded keys.

sections.s2_technical:
The happy path is a nested loop. `describe_instances()` returns a dictionary with a `Reservations` key; each reservation has an `Instances` key; each instance is a dictionary with fields like `InstanceId`, `State`, and `Tags`. So you write `for reservation in response["Reservations"]: for instance in reservation["Instances"]:` and read each instance. This works for a tiny account but fails quietly as the account grows, which is exactly why a production script layers several concerns on top.

Pagination is the first and most important addition. The EC2 API returns at most a page of results and a `NextToken` when more exist. If you ignore the token you silently process only the first page, which is a classic cause of broken automation that "worked in dev but missed instances in prod." The production fix is to use a Boto3 paginator: `paginator = ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances")` and then iterate `paginator.paginate()`, which transparently follows `NextToken` until every page is consumed, so you never get incomplete results.

Error handling turns a fragile script into a dependable one. AWS calls can fail transiently with throttling or timeouts, or permanently with an access-denied or invalid-parameter error. A production script wraps calls in try/except for `botocore.exceptions.ClientError`, inspects the error code, retries transient errors with exponential backoff (Boto3's built-in retry config helps, and you can add your own for application-level retries), and surfaces permission errors clearly instead of crashing with a stack trace. This means a brief throttle does not abort a long inventory run, and a missing IAM permission produces an actionable message.

Server-side filtering means asking AWS to return only what you need rather than downloading everything and filtering in Python. You pass a `Filters` argument, for example filtering by tag or instance state, so the API returns a smaller result set. This is faster, cheaper, and less error-prone than pulling thousands of instances across the network and discarding most of them. Logging adds a structured, timestamped record of what the script did — how many instances it saw, which it acted on, and any errors — using Python's logging module at appropriate levels, which is essential for audit and debugging in a bank.

Finally, credentials must come from the default credential-provider chain, not hardcoded keys. On EC2 or EKS the script should run under an IAM role (an instance profile or an IRSA role) and let Boto3 pick up temporary, automatically rotated credentials from the environment, the shared config, or the instance metadata service. You never embed access keys in the code or a config file, because hardcoded keys leak, do not rotate, and are a serious security finding in a banking environment. A senior nuance is to also set an explicit region, use least-privilege IAM policies scoped to the exact actions and resources, and make the script idempotent and read-only unless remediation is explicitly intended.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India platform team needs a reliable inventory of production EC2 instances. A quick script that reads only the first page and crashes on a throttle is dangerous because it gives a false, incomplete picture of what is running.

Problem 1 — The account has far more instances than fit in one API page, so a single `describe_instances()` call misses most of them. This is exactly what a paginator solves: follow `NextToken` until all pages are read.

Problem 2 — Occasional throttling and the risk of a missing permission must not abort the run or crash unhelpfully. We add error handling with retries for transient errors and clear messages for permission errors.

Problem 3 — We only care about production instances and must keep an audit log and use the IAM role, not keys. We filter server-side by the Environment tag, log structured progress, and rely on the credential-provider chain. Because this document's runnable code standard is Java, we model the same production concerns in a Java simulation of a paginated AWS client: classes `AwsInstance`, `InstancePage`, `FakeEc2Client` (returns pages with a next-token), `InstanceInventory` (paginates, retries, filters, logs), and an `Ec2InventoryDemo` main. The real Boto3 Python is shown alongside as the production reference.

##### 4b. Boto3 Production Reference (Python)

```python
# ─── File: scripts/list_instances.py ───
# National Bank of India — production EC2 inventory with Boto3.
import logging
import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)-7s] %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("nbi.inventory")

def list_production_instances(region="ap-south-1"):
    # Credentials come from the default provider chain (IAM role / instance
    # profile / IRSA) — NEVER hardcoded keys. Built-in adaptive retries added.
    cfg = Config(region_name=region, retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})
    ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", config=cfg)

    # Paginator transparently follows NextToken — no incomplete results.
    paginator = ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances")
    # Server-side filter: only running Production instances come back.
    page_iter = paginator.paginate(Filters=[
        {"Name": "tag:Environment", "Values": ["Production"]},
        {"Name": "instance-state-name", "Values": ["running"]},
    ])

    found = []
    try:
        for page in page_iter:                      # iterate ALL pages
            for reservation in page["Reservations"]:
                for inst in reservation["Instances"]:
                    iid = inst["InstanceId"]
                    found.append(iid)
                    log.info("Found %s type=%s state=%s",
                             iid, inst["InstanceType"], inst["State"]["Name"])
    except ClientError as e:
        code = e.response["Error"]["Code"]
        if code in ("UnauthorizedOperation", "AccessDenied"):
            log.error("Permission denied — check IAM policy: %s", code)
        else:
            log.error("AWS error while listing instances: %s", code)
        raise
    log.info("Total production instances: %d", len(found))
    return found

if __name__ == "__main__":
    list_production_instances()
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a request to list all running Production instances in the account.

Step 1 — The inventory starts with a null token and fetches page one. The fake client returns two instances — one Production running and one Development running — plus a next-token indicating more pages exist.

Step 2 — The inventory filters page one server-side style: it keeps the Production running instance and skips the Development one, logging the kept instance.

Step 3 — Because a next-token was returned, the inventory fetches page two. The fake client throttles on the first attempt, so the retry logic logs a warning and waits with exponential backoff, then retries and succeeds.

Step 4 — Page two returns two Production instances, one running and one stopped. The inventory keeps the running one and skips the stopped one, and sees a null next-token, meaning this was the last page.

Step 5 — With no more pages, the inventory logs the total count of Production running instances and returns the complete list to the caller — complete precisely because pagination was followed and the transient throttle was retried rather than aborting the run.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [INFO   ] NBI EC2 inventory — paginate + retry + filter + log (IAM role credentials)
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [INFO   ] Found i-0a1 type=m5.large state=running
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [WARNING] Throttled on page 2 — retry 1 after 100ms
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [INFO   ] Found i-0b1 type=m5.xlarge state=running
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [INFO   ] Total production running instances: 2
2026-10-30 02:25:00 [INFO   ] Returning 2 production instances to caller.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  listProduction() request (IAM role credentials from provider chain)
    │
    ▼
  token=null ──▶ describeInstances(null)
    │              returns page1 [i-0a1 Prod/run, i-0a2 Dev/run] + TOKEN-PAGE-2
    │ filter: keep Production+running → i-0a1
    ▼
  token=TOKEN-PAGE-2 ──▶ describeInstances(token)
    │   1st attempt → ThrottlingException
    │   retry w/ backoff (100ms → 200ms …)
    │   2nd attempt → page2 [i-0b1 Prod/run, i-0b2 Prod/stopped] + null
    │ filter: keep i-0b1 (running), skip i-0b2 (stopped)
    ▼
  token=null → stop pagination
    │
    ▼
  return [i-0a1, i-0b1]  (COMPLETE — no page missed, throttle survived)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To iterate EC2 instances with Boto3 I call describe_instances, which returns a dictionary where the top-level Reservations list contains Instances lists, so the happy path is a nested loop: for each reservation, for each instance, read fields like the instance id, type, and state. That is fine for a toy, but a production script has to add several things because the simple version silently fails as the account grows. The single most important addition is pagination: the EC2 API returns only one page plus a NextToken when more results exist, and if you ignore that token you process only the first page, which is the classic reason automation "works in dev but misses instances in prod." I use a Boto3 paginator so it transparently follows NextToken until every page is read.

Next I add error handling. AWS calls can fail transiently with throttling or permanently with access-denied, so I wrap calls to catch ClientError, inspect the error code, retry transient errors with exponential backoff, and surface permission errors with an actionable message instead of a raw stack trace, so a brief throttle never aborts a long inventory run. I filter server-side by passing a Filters argument — for example by the Environment tag and instance state — so AWS returns only the Production running instances I care about rather than me downloading thousands and discarding most in Python, which is faster, cheaper, and less error-prone. I add structured, timestamped logging of how many instances were seen and any errors, because in a bank every automation run needs an audit trail.

Finally, and this is non-negotiable in banking, credentials come from the default credential-provider chain — an IAM role via an instance profile or IRSA — so Boto3 picks up temporary, automatically rotated credentials, and I never hardcode access keys, which leak and do not rotate. In my project at the National Bank of India this inventory ran under a least-privilege IAM role scoped to describe-instances, used a paginator so no instance was ever missed, retried throttles with backoff, filtered to Production running instances server-side, and logged every result for audit. The principle I always state is that the difference between a demo and a production script is pagination, error handling with retries, server-side filtering, structured logging, and role-based credentials — the happy-path nested loop is only the beginning.
